query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In single‐phase high-entropy alloys, brittle behavior emerges not from the typical coarse precipitates seen in conventional alloys but from thermal-history–induced modifications of the grain-boundary chemistry. Specifically, extended moderate-temperature annealing promotes localized solute segregation and transient, nanoscale grain-boundary precipitation, which in turn leads to intergranular decohesion and brittleness, whereas short-term high-temperature annealing minimizes these effects and preserves ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: An initially single-phase high-entropy alloy with compositionally complex homogeneous matrix (e.g., a CoCrFeMnNi-type alloy).
generation.intervention: Apply controlled thermal annealing with two distinct regimes: (a) short-term high-temperature annealing that minimizes grain-boundary diffusion and segregation, and (b) prolonged moderate-temperature annealing designed to promote grain-boundary solute segregation and transient precipitation.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted under service-relevant temperatures. The low-temperature embrittlement regime is tested via fracture and tensile tests at ambient to sub-ambient temperatures, while high-temperature service conditions are simulated by tests at elevated temperatures where diffusion kinetics are significant.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain-boundary microstructure modifications, specifically the development of solute-enriched regions and transient nanoscale precipitates along the boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Thermal exposure under prolonged moderate-temperature annealing increases local diffusion along grain boundaries, leading to segregation of specific alloying elements. This localized change alters the cohesive strength of the boundaries and encourages intergranular fracture, thereby manifesting brittle behavior even without the formation of large, classical precipitates found in conventional alloys.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloy samples subjected to prolonged moderate-temperature annealing will exhibit lower fracture toughness, increased intergranular cracking, and reduced ductility when compared to samples receiving short-term high-temperature annealing, which should retain a more uniform grain-boundary chemistry and thus higher toughness.
generation.baseline: Alloy samples processed with minimal thermal exposure (or under conditions that inhibit grain-boundary diffusion) serving as a ductile reference state with uniformly distributed solutes.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is predicted to operate under service conditions that allow significant grain-boundary diffusion (i.e., moderate temperatures over extended times), and may not be as significant under high strain-rate or short-duration thermal exposures where diffusion is limited.
generation.uncertainty: The precise thermal processing window and the quantitative relationship between annealing parameters (time and temperature), extent of grain-boundary segregation/precipitation, and the resulting embrittlement require detailed experimental calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of identical single-phase high-entropy alloy samples. Subject one group to short-term high-temperature annealing (control condition) and the other group to prolonged moderate-temperature annealing designed to encourage grain-boundary solute diffusion. After processing, perform in situ fracture toughness and tensile tests under both ambient and elevated temperatures. Conduct atom probe tomography (APT) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to characterize grain-boundary chemistry and detect any nanoscale precipitate formation.
measurements: Fracture toughness (K_IC) and tensile ductility measurements under controlled loading conditions.
Microscopic analysis (APT/TEM) of grain-boundary composition and presence of transient precipitates.
Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) to map grain-boundary structure and identify regions of intergranular decohesion.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples subjected to prolonged moderate-temperature annealing do not show a statistically significant reduction in fracture toughness (or do not exhibit evidence of localized grain-boundary segregation/precipitation) compared to the short-term high-temperature annealed control, then the hypothesis that these thermal conditions drive brittle behavior via grain-boundary modification is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The presence of intermetallic compounds, such as brittle Laves phases, typically reduces the ductility of RHEAs (), prompting extensive efforts to develop single-phase RHEAs for high-temperature applications (, , , , , , ). The equiatomic Ti-V-Nb-Ta alloy is one of the most attractive RHEAs, which solidifies as a single-phase body-centered cubic (BCC) microstructure with heterogeneous elemental distribution and exhibits excellent high-temperature strength and room-temperature ductility (). Equimolar Ti-V-Nb-Ta has an extremely high compressive yield strength, 1273 MPa at room temperature and 688 MPa at 900°C (). By comparison, conventional high-temperature Ni-base superalloys notably soften above 600°C, with the compressive yield strength dropping to ~200 MPa at 900°C (). Equimolar Ti-V-Nb-Ta also exhibits impressive tensile ductility, ~14% at room temperature (), and a relatively low brittle-to-ductile transition temperature between −47° and −27°C, comparable to BCC metals and stainless steels for engineering applications (, ). ABSTRACTIn this study, tensile and creep deformation of a high-entropy alloy processed by selective laser melting (SLM) has been investigated; hot ductility drop was identified at first, and the loss of ductility at elevated temperature was associated with intergranular fracture. By modifying the grain boundary morphology from straight to serration, the hot ductility drop issue has been resolved successfully. The serrated grain boundary could be achieved by reducing the cooling rate of solution heat treatment, which allowed the coarsening of L12 structured γ′ precipitates to interfere with mobile grain boundaries, resulting in undulation of the grain boundary morphology. Tensile and creep tests at 650°C were conducted, and serrated grain boundary could render a significant increase in tensile fracture strain and creep rupture life by a factor of 3.5 and 400, respectively. Detailed microstructure analysis has indicated that serrated grain boundary could distribute strains more evenly than that of straight morphology.
